An instrument workshop tried putting jobs waiting for parts and jobs ready for work on one schedule. Six weeks later its manager approved the schedule for new jobs – and explains what the team had to agree before it was useful, and what would get more time next round.

By Thomas Barregren

Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments, used to keep its jobs on two paper sheets: one for jobs awaiting parts, another for jobs ready for work. In January 2026 the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule from Benchline, chosen after checking that it could tell those statuses apart. Workshop manager Priya Vale describes what the trial settled and what she would change.

## The workshop wrote the rules before setup

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. Collection arrangements stayed outside the schedule: the team continued to discuss them with customers by telephone.

Asked in an email interview what had to be settled before the schedule was useful, Vale pointed to a single status:

'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'

The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. ## Vale on the next round

Asked whether the choice would be the same again, and what would change, Vale answered:

'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'

Managers weighing a similar trial can begin with the question Fenwick had to settle: what each status means, and who updates it.

# Fenwick keeps shared bench schedule for new repair jobs

An instrument workshop tried putting jobs waiting for parts and jobs ready for work on one schedule. Six weeks later its manager approved the schedule for new jobs – and explains what the team had to agree before it was useful, and what would get more time next round.

By Thomas Barregren

Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments, used to keep its jobs on two paper sheets: one for jobs awaiting parts, another for jobs ready for work. In January 2026 the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule from Benchline, chosen after checking that it could tell those statuses apart. Workshop manager Priya Vale describes what the trial settled and what she would change.

## The workshop wrote the rules before setup

The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. Collection arrangements stayed outside the schedule: the team continued to discuss them with customers by telephone.

Asked in an email interview what had to be settled before the schedule was useful, Vale pointed to a single status:

'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'

## A record of 38 jobs, without speed figures

The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction, so it documents the team's experience rather than any measured change in repair speed.

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## Vale on the next round

Asked whether the choice would be the same again, and what would change, Vale answered:

'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'

Managers weighing a similar trial can begin with the question Fenwick had to settle: what each status means, and who updates it.
EOF

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. Its jobs awaiting parts and its jobs ready for work used to appear on separate paper sheets. In January 2026 the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule from Benchline, chosen after checking that it could tell those statuses apart. Workshop manager Priya Vale explains what the team had to settle first, and names one thing to change.

## The workshop set its own status rules

Benchline configured the workshop's choices and trained four staff in one online session. Those choices were which statuses to use and who would update them. The team continued to discuss collection arrangements with customers by telephone.

Asked in an email interview on 2 March 2026 what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale wrote:

'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'

## The trial summary leaves repair speed unmeasured

The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction. What it documents is the team's reported experience, not a measured change in how fast repairs are done.

## Vale looks back on the trial

The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions. Asked whether the choice would be the same again, and what would change, Vale wrote:

'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'

# Source-comparison report

Draft: `scratch/write-run.OzdNqy/draft.md`
Source: `work/source.md` (Brief + Material)
Language: British English (en_GB). Source language English. No translated quotations.

The byline "By Thomas Barregren" comes from the invocation. It is not assessed.

## A. Claim accounting

Each item gives the draft passage, then the source passage in the source's own words, then what differs and the verdict.

### Title

1. **Draft:** "Fenwick keeps shared bench schedule for new jobs"
   **Source:** "The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
   **Difference:** The draft says "keeps". The source says "approved continued use". A headline in the present tense conventionally reports a recent decision, so "keeps" reads as "decided to keep". The draft makes Fenwick the subject where the source has the manager, but the manager approved use on the workshop's behalf. The scope "for new jobs" is preserved.
   **Verdict:** Supported. No finding.

### Standfirst

2. **Draft:** "Jobs waiting for parts and jobs ready for work used to sit on separate paper sheets at one instrument workshop."
   **Source:** "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets." Also: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments."
   **Verdict:** Supported. No finding.

3. **Draft:** "After a six-week trial of a single schedule"
   **Source:** "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule."
   - **"single" for "shared":** "a shared bench schedule" is one schedule. It replaced the separate sheets ("Previously ..."), and Benchline was chosen because "it could distinguish these statuses". The draft does not carry the word "shared", but it does not contradict it. No finding.
   - **"After":** see Finding 1.

4. **Draft:** "its manager explains what the team had to agree before the schedule was useful"
   **Source:** Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant."
   **Difference:** None of substance. The presupposition that the schedule became useful is in the interviewer's question, and Vale answered it without objecting.
   **Verdict:** Supported. No finding.

5. **Draft:** "and what would get an extra week"
   **Source:** "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
   **Difference:** None. "would" is kept conditional.
   **Verdict:** Supported. No finding.

### Paragraph 1

6. **Draft:** "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments."
   **Source:** identical sentence.
   **Verdict:** Supported.

7. **Draft:** "Its jobs awaiting parts and its jobs ready for work used to appear on separate paper sheets."
   **Source:** "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets."
   **Verdict:** Supported.

8. **Draft:** "In January 2026 the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule from Benchline, chosen after checking that it could tell those statuses apart."
   **Source:** "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses." "Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff." The brief says: "scheduling software supplier Benchline".
   **Difference:**
   - "from Benchline": the schedule is Benchline's. This follows from the chosen supplier, which configured the statuses and trained the staff.
   - The draft's passive "chosen after checking" leaves out who checked (the team) but does not change it.
   - The draft leaves the timing of the choice relative to the trial unstated, as the source does.
   **Verdict:** Supported. No finding.

9. **Draft:** "Workshop manager Priya Vale explains what the team had to settle first, and names one thing to change."
   **Source:** "workshop manager Priya Vale". Question: "what would you change?" Answer: "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
   **Difference:** Vale gave exactly one change, so "names one thing" matches.
   **Verdict:** Supported.

### Heading: "The workshop set its own status rules"

10. **Source:** "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices."
    **Difference:** "status rules" is a fair summary of the statuses plus who updates them. "its own" contrasts the workshop with Benchline, as the source does.
    **Verdict:** Supported.

### Paragraph 2

11. **Draft:** "Benchline configured the workshop's choices and trained four staff in one online session."
    **Source:** "Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session."
    **Verdict:** Supported.

12. **Draft:** "The workshop itself had defined the statuses and decided who would update them."
    **Source:** "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them."
    **Difference:** The past perfect puts the definition before the configuration. "configured those choices" presupposes that the choices already existed.
    **Verdict:** Supported.

13. **Draft:** "The team continued to discuss collection arrangements with customers by telephone."
    **Source:** "The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers."
    **Verdict:** Supported.

14. **Draft:** "Asked in an email interview on 2 March 2026 what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale wrote:"
    **Source:** "email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale". Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?"
    **Difference:** "wrote" correctly reflects the email medium ("No ... spoken exchange ... is recorded"). The draft does not name the interviewer, which is an omission, not a change.
    **Verdict:** Supported.

15. **Quotation:** 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'
    **Source:** "We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench."
    **Difference:** Verbatim. Only the quotation marks change (British single quotes). Publication is approved ("Publication of the extract was approved by Vale").
    **Verdict:** Supported.

### Heading: "The trial summary leaves repair speed unmeasured"

16. **Source:** "It does not measure repair duration" and "not a measured improvement in repair speed".
    **Verdict:** Supported.

### Paragraph 3

17. **Draft:** "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts."
    **Source:** identical in substance.
    **Verdict:** Supported.

18. **Draft:** "It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction."
    **Source:** identical.
    **Verdict:** Supported.

19. **Draft:** "What it documents is the team's reported experience, not a measured change in how fast repairs are done."
    **Source:** "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop."
    **Difference:**
    - *Subject.* The source names the summary and the interview together. The draft names the summary alone. The summary is one of the two, and its content ("It says staff could see ...") is reported experience. The "X, not Y" frame contrasts the two rather than claiming the list is exhaustive.
    - *Improvement vs change.* The draft's "change" is broader than the source's "improvement". It is still covered by "It does not measure repair duration", so no measured change of any kind exists in the summary.
    **Verdict:** Supported. No finding.

### Heading: "Vale looks back on the trial"

20. See Finding 1. The heading presents the trial as finished.

### Paragraph 4

21. **Draft:** "The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
    **Source:** identical.
    **Verdict:** Supported.

22. **Draft:** "Asked whether the choice would be the same again, and what would change, Vale wrote:"
    **Source:** Question: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?"
    **Difference:** The draft paraphrases the question impersonally. "what would change" is slightly looser than "what would you change", but in context the quote that follows fixes the meaning as what Vale would change.
    **Verdict:** Supported. No finding.

23. **Quotation:** 'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'
    **Source:** verbatim.
    **Verdict:** Supported.

### Final paragraph

24. **Draft:** "Managers weighing a similar trial can begin with the question Fenwick had to settle: what each status means, and who updates it."
    **Source:** "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them." Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant." Also: "The summary and interview establish ... not ... a recommendation for every workshop."
    **Difference:**
    - The factual premise is broadened. See Finding 2.
    - The advice is the author's own. See Editorial question E1.

### Pronoun accounting (person, number, natural gender)

| Pronoun | Referent | Features | Source basis | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| "its manager" (standfirst) | the workshop | 3rd singular, neuter, no natural gender | "workshop manager Priya Vale" | Supported |
| "Its jobs" (para 1) | Fenwick Instrument Repairs | 3rd singular, neuter | the workshop's jobs | Supported |
| "it could tell those statuses apart" | Benchline / its schedule | 3rd singular, neuter | "checking that it could distinguish these statuses" | Supported |
| "update them" | the statuses | 3rd plural, neuter | "who would update them" | Supported |
| "It says" / "It does not" / "What it documents" | the trial summary | 3rd singular, neuter | "It says" / "It does not measure" | Supported |
| "its status definitions" | the team | 3rd singular collective, neuter | "its status definitions" | Supported |
| "who updates it" | each status | 3rd singular, neuter | "decided who would update them" | Supported |
| "We", "I", "it" inside the quotations | Vale's own wording | 1st plural (team including Vale); 1st singular (Vale); "it" = a part / the schedule | verbatim | Supported |

The draft uses no personal pronoun for Priya Vale anywhere, so it asserts no natural gender. The material gives none, so nothing is added. Every "its" and "it" in the draft refers to a thing, so there are no grammatical-gender issues in English.

## B. Findings: source support

### Finding 1: the trial is presented as finished before the interview (timing)

**Draft passages:**
- Standfirst: "After a six-week trial of a single schedule, its manager explains ..."
- Heading: "Vale looks back on the trial"

**Source:**
- "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial"
- "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026"
- "an email interview on 2 March 2026"

**What differs:** The source gives only the month the trial began. Six weeks from a start in late January ends in early to mid-March. The draft states that Vale's explanation (the 2 March interview) came after the trial, and the heading presents the trial as already over.

**Concrete case:** The trial begins on 26 January 2026 and runs to 9 March 2026. The 23 February summary is an interim summary, and the manager's approval and the 2 March interview both fall within the trial. This fits every supplied statement. The source says nothing about when the trial ended or that the summary was a final one, so no quoted statement rules the case out. In this case the draft's "After a six-week trial" is false.

**Smallest supported repair:**
- Standfirst: replace "After a six-week trial of a single schedule, its manager explains ..." with "In a six-week trial of a single schedule, the team had to agree ... ; its manager explains ...". Alternatively, and more simply: "Asked about a six-week trial of a single schedule, its manager explains ...".
- Heading: replace "Vale looks back on the trial" with, for example, "What Vale would change".

This is a minor finding. If the author can confirm that the trial ended before 2 March, the draft may stand.

### Finding 2: final paragraph broadens what Fenwick "had to settle"

**Draft passage:** "... can begin with the question Fenwick had to settle: what each status means, and who updates it."

**Source:**
- Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant."
- Material: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them."

**What differs:**
- *Necessity ("had to").* Vale presents only the meaning of *ready for work* as something the team had to agree before the schedule was useful. The line between that advice and a recommendation the material says it does not establish is still unsettled. The editor should decide whether a closing recommendation belongs in a case whose material expressly stops short of one. If it is kept, the repaired wording from Finding 2 is sufficient.

## D. Translation findings

# Source-comparison report: Fenwick case draft

Draft: scratch/write-run.OzdNqy/draft.md
Source: work/source.md (Brief + Material)
Language: British English (en_GB); source English; no quotation translated. Translation checks therefore do not apply. The byline "By Thomas Barregren" comes from the invocation and is not a finding.

## Claim accounting

Each pair gives the draft passage, the source passage in the source's words, and any difference with its two-way test.

### Title
1. Draft: "Fenwick keeps shared bench schedule for new jobs"
   Source: "The manager approved continued use for new jobs"; Vale: "I would use it again for new jobs."
   Difference: the draft names the actor as Fenwick where the source names the manager, and "keeps" is present tense where the source says "approved". The scope "for new jobs" is kept. The manager decides for the workshop, and a news headline normally reports the latest known status. The only counter-case is a reversal after 2 March, and nothing in the material suggests one, so the headline is defensible as written. No finding.

### Standfirst
2. Draft: "Jobs waiting for parts and jobs ready for work used to sit on separate paper sheets at one instrument workshop."
   Source: "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets."
   Difference: none of substance. "One instrument workshop" is supported by "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments." No finding.
3. Draft: "Asked about a six-week trial of a single schedule, its manager explains what the team had to agree before the schedule was useful"
   Source: "a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule"; Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?"; Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant."
   Difference: the draft says "single" where the source says "shared". The case to test is several schedules being used. It is excluded by "a shared bench schedule" (one schedule) and by "could distinguish these statuses" (both statuses sit in one system). "Agree" is Vale's own verb. "Its" refers to the workshop and is singular and neuter; it carries no natural gender. "Explains" matches an email answer. No finding.
4. Draft: "and what would get an extra week."
   Source: Vale: "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
   Difference: "extra week" renders "another week", and the draft points to what Vale said would get it. The modality stays conditional ("would"). No finding.

### Opening paragraph
5. Draft: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments." The source says the same word for word. No finding.
6. Draft: "Its jobs awaiting parts and its jobs ready for work used to appear on separate paper sheets."
   Source: the same passage as item 2. "Its" refers to Fenwick and is singular and neuter. No finding.
7. Draft: "In January 2026 the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule from Benchline, chosen after checking that it could tell those statuses apart."
   Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses."
   Difference: the passive "chosen" leaves out who chose, and the context shows it was the team. "It" refers to Benchline, as in the source, and is singular and neuter. No finding.
8. Draft: "Workshop manager Priya Vale explains what the team had to settle first, and names one thing to change."
   Source: the question "What did the team have to settle…" and the question "what would you change?", answered with "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
   Difference: "names one thing" matches the single change she gave. The draft uses no personal pronoun for Vale, so it asserts no natural gender. No finding.

### Section "The workshop set its own status rules"
9. Heading, "The workshop set its own status rules". Source: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them."
   Difference: "status rules" sums up defining the statuses and assigning who updates them. It names the same thing. No finding.
10. Draft: "Benchline configured the workshop's choices and trained four staff in one online session." The source says the same in substance ("Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session"). No finding.
11. Draft: "The workshop itself had defined the statuses and decided who would update them."
   Source: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices…"
   Difference: the pluperfect puts the definition before the configuration. That order is supported because "configured those choices" presupposes choices that already existed. No finding.
12. Draft: "The team continued to discuss collection arrangements with customers by telephone."
   Source: "The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers." Same meaning. No finding.
13. Draft: "Asked in an email interview on 2 March 2026 what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, Vale wrote:"
   Source: "email interview on 2 March 2026 between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale"; Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?"
   Difference: "wrote" is supported because the interview was by email. No finding.
14. Quotation: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'
   Source: identical wording. Only the quotation marks changed, to British single quotes. The pronouns ("We", "it") are unchanged. No finding.

### Section "The trial summary leaves repair speed unmeasured"
15. Heading. Source: "It does not measure repair duration". Same thing. No finding.
16. Draft: "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts."
   Source: the same wording. The draft adds no evaluation of the count. No finding.
17. Draft: "It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction." The source says the same word for word. No finding.
18. Draft: "What it documents is the team's reported experience, not a measured change in how fast repairs are done."
   Source: "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop."
   Difference: the draft credits this to the summary alone, where the source credits the summary and interview together. It also says "measured change" where the source says "measured improvement". The source's statement covers the summary, so what the draft says about the summary is within the source's own description. "Change" is wider than "improvement", but "It does not measure repair duration" rules out any measured change in speed, so no case exists in which the draft fails. No finding.

### Section "Vale on making the same choice again"
19. Draft: "The manager approved continued use for new jobs, but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions." The source says the same word for word. No finding.
20. Draft: "Asked whether the choice would be the same again, and what would change, Vale wrote:"
   Source: Question: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?" Same content. No finding.
21. Quotation: 'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'
   Source: identical wording. The modality ("would") is kept. No finding.

### Closing
22. Draft: "Managers weighing a similar trial can begin with the choices Fenwick made: what each status means, and who updates it."
   Source: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them"; Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant."; Material: "The summary and interview establish … not … a recommendation for every workshop."; Brief: "No author name or call to action is supplied."
   Difference: the facts are supported. Fenwick did define the statuses and decide who updates them, and "it" refers to each status. The sentence itself is the writer's own advice to the target readers, and it rests on Vale's reported experience. It is permissive ("can begin with") rather than prescriptive, and it is limited to managers weighing a similar trial. It does not claim that the approach works for every workshop. The material explicitly says it establishes no recommendation for every workshop, however, and the brief supplies no call to action. Whether this line counts as supported advocacy or as a recommendation the material disclaims is genuinely unsettled. It is reported below as an editorial question, not as a defect.

## Findings

### Source-support findings
None. No draft claim lacks a supporting source passage, and none changes the subject, scope, time, modality, certainty or the person who asserts it in a way that a concrete case compatible with the material would expose.

### Translation findings
None applicable. The source is English, the target is British English, and no quotation is translated.

### Editorial question (not a defect)
- Closing sentence (item 22): "Managers weighing a similar trial can begin with the choices Fenwick made…" is the draft's own advice. The material states that it does not establish "a recommendation for every workshop", and the brief supplies no call to action. The sentence is permissive and limited in scope, so it is defensible as advocacy resting on Vale's reported experience. The editor should decide whether Benchline wants a closing pointer of this kind. If not, the smallest supported alternative ties it to Fenwick's own account, for example: "At Fenwick, the first choices were what each status meant and who would update it."

## Completion status
Complete. Every factual and attributed claim in the title, standfirst, headings, body and quotations is accounted for. No source-support or translation findings are unresolved. One editorial question, the closing sentence, is left open for editorial decision.
